title: Shvetaketu and the word that points
word: the Gayatri and the peace chants
hookLine: a proud son, a cup of salt water, and the Gayatri's first word
carry: hindus point to brahman as tat: that
tomorrow: of Savitr: is that the sun, or something behind the sun?

lines: A TEXT THAT JUST SAYS: THAT ONE.
THE NOUN IS A LINE AWAY.
cards: A text arrives with no photo and no link, just two words: that one. So you scroll up, hunting for whatever that is. The Gayatri opens the same way.
Its first word is tat, that. And the thing it points at doesn't show up next. Two more words go by, the line ends, and only at the start of the next line does the noun arrive.
Why would a prayer begin by pointing?

teach.h: TAT POINTS TO BHARGO, A LINE AWAY.
teach.b: First the reader's answer. Tat is the neuter form of that, and the next neuter noun is bhargo, radiance, a line away. Varenyam matches too, like teammates in the same jersey.
So the grammar says: that radiance. But Hindus care about this small word for a bigger reason. Tat is how the tradition points at God.
In the Chandogya Upanishad, a boy named Shvetaketu comes home at twenty-four after twelve years of study, proud, sure he knows it all.
His father, Uddalaka, asks one question: did you learn the thing by which the unheard becomes heard? He hadn't. So the father teaches with what's at hand.

teach.h: SALT IN WATER: IN EVERY DROP.
teach.b: Put this salt in water, he says, and bring it to me in the morning. The salt is gone; the boy can't find it. Sip from the top, says the father.
From the bottom. Salty. You can't see it, but it's in every drop.

teach.h: TAT TVAM ASI: THAT, YOU ARE.
teach.b: That fine thing in everything is the real, the self, he says, and then the line Hindus have repeated ever since: tat tvam asi.

teach.h: GOD IS POINTED AT, NOT HELD.
teach.b: This is Brahman, the one reality, and it can't be held up like a cup on a table, so the teachers point: that. The Gita gives three words for Brahman, Om tat sat, and tat is the middle one.
In the Gayatri, the grammar only points to the radiance. Many teachers hear the same reach in it: the verse begins by turning toward what's bigger than the one saying it.

how: Teachers who explain the Gayatri word by word often begin with tat and show how it waits for bhargo, the radiance. Hindus also use tat for Brahman, as in Om tat sat and the Chandogya's tat tvam asi.

games.q: what does “the gayatri and the peace chants” mean?
o: a king who named his son after the sun
a boy who learned every Veda by heart in a single year
a proud son, a cup of salt water, and a small word that points

games.q: what points where — tap the pairs.
p: radiance: the noun tat waits for
that, you are: Uddalaka to his son
three words for Brahman, in the Gita

s: in the Gayatri, tat is a name of God
there it points to bhargo, the radiance. elsewhere Hindus do use tat for Brahman: Om tat sat.
Uddalaka taught his son with salt dissolved in water
unseen, but in every sip: tat tvam asi.
it points away: that, over there.

games.q: Sam asks why Hindus would call God 'that' instead of a name. which answer comes from the Upanishad?
o: it's rude in Sanskrit to say God's name out loud.
Brahman is in everything, like salt in water, so you point instead of holding it up.
Sanskrit had no word for God.
games.why: Uddalaka showed his son the salt he couldn't see but could taste in every drop: tat tvam asi, that, you are.

practice: Let your eyes rest on the farthest thing you can see: a window, a doorway, the far wall. Silently call it only that, without naming it.
If you have a glass of water near you, take one slow sip and remember the salt you couldn't see. Stay facing toward that while the time runs.

wordCard.voice: The Gayatri and the peace chants. Today's piece: tat, that, the word that waits a line for its noun, and the word Hindus point to Brahman with.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: tat, that, the first word of the Gayatri verse.

carryVoice: The line to take with you: Hindus point to Brahman as tat: that, because it is in everything. That, you are. That's day fifteen hundred.
